subject: mlops
question: Does billing stop when the training job finishes?

artifact.description:
A data scientist launched an 8-GPU instance (Rs 2,500/hour) for a 6-hour training run on Friday and went home; the notebook finished at 22:00.
AI: "Cloud billing stops when the job finishes."

ai_claim: Yes. The cloud charges for compute used, and compute stops being used when the job finishes, so billing stops.

ai_solution.text: Cloud billing is usage-based.
The training job finished at 22:00.
After that, no compute is used.
So billing stops.

failure.misconception: Confusing job completion with instance termination
failure.explanation: Instances are billed while running, whether or not a job is active. The idle instance runs all weekend: about 58 hours x Rs 2,500 = Rs 1,45,000 for nothing. Use managed training jobs that release hardware on completion, auto-shutdown for idle notebooks, and budget alerts.
failure.why_convincing: 'Pay for what you use' suggests billing follows activity.

canonical_solution: No: the instance is billed until it is stopped. Use managed jobs or idle auto-shutdown.

valid_evidence.summary: Friday 22:00 to Monday 08:00 is 58 hours at Rs 2,500/hour = Rs 1,45,000.
VM instances bill per running second regardless of utilisation.

counterexamples: The weekend bill for an idle instance exceeds the training cost many times over.

hints.text: Ask what the cloud bills for.
Step 3 equates idle with unbilled.
Instances bill while running, not while busy.
Compute the weekend cost.
Step 3 is wrong: the running instance keeps billing.

repair: Use managed training jobs, idle auto-shutdown and budget alerts.
debrief: In the cloud, the expensive mistakes are forgotten resources. Automate shutdown.

subject: mlops
question: Is the notebook server effectively private because its IP is not publicised?

artifact.description:
A Jupyter server runs on a cloud VM with a public IP, port 8888 open to 0.0.0.0/0, and token authentication disabled 'to make access easier'. The VM has an IAM role with access to the training-data bucket.
AI: "Nobody knows the IP address, so it's effectively private."

ai_claim: Yes. The IP address has not been shared with anyone, so no one else will find the server.

ai_solution.text: The server has a public IP.
The IP has not been shared.
People cannot connect to an address they don't know.
So the server is effectively private.

failure.misconception: Relying on an unknown IP for security
failure.explanation: Internet-wide scanners probe every IPv4 address continuously; open Jupyter servers are found within hours and give attackers a shell with the VM's IAM role - including the training data. Keep notebooks off public IPs (VPN or identity-aware proxy), require authentication, and scope IAM roles narrowly.

canonical_solution: No: scanners find open ports quickly, and an unauthenticated Jupyter gives code execution. Remove public access and require auth.

valid_evidence.summary: Search engines for exposed services index open Jupyter servers by port and banner.
Unauthenticated remote code execution endpoints must never be internet-exposed.

counterexamples: An attacker runs code as the VM and downloads the training bucket.

hints.text: Ask how attackers find servers.
Step 3 assumes an unknown IP is hidden.
Internet scanning makes obscurity useless.
Consider what Jupyter access allows.
Step 3 is wrong: open ports are scanned. Require auth and remove public access.

repair: Put notebooks behind a VPN or identity-aware proxy, enable authentication and limit IAM scope.
debrief: Notebook servers are remote shells. Treat them with the same security as SSH.

subject: mlops
question: Will the job finish at 70% lower cost?

artifact.description:
A 30-hour training job runs on spot GPU instances (70% cheaper) without saving checkpoints.
Spot instances in this region are typically reclaimed after 4-12 hours.
AI: "Spot instances give the same result for 70% less."

ai_claim: Yes. Spot instances run the same hardware at a 70% discount, so the job finishes at 70% lower cost.

ai_solution.text: Spot GPUs are the same hardware.
They cost 70% less.
The job runs for 30 hours either way.
So it finishes at 70% lower cost.

failure.explanation: Spot instances can be reclaimed at short notice. With reclaims after 4-12 hours and no checkpoints, each interruption loses all progress, so a 30-hour job may never finish - costs accumulate with no result. Save checkpoints regularly (e.g. every 30 minutes to object storage) and resume automatically on a new instance.
failure.why_convincing: The discount is real and the hardware is identical.

canonical_solution: No: without checkpoints, reclaims restart the job from scratch, possibly forever. Checkpoint and resume.

valid_evidence.summary: Reclaims typically occur after 4-12 hours; the job needs 30 hours.
Interruptible compute requires checkpointing and automatic resume.

counterexamples: After three reclaims, the job has used 25 hours and completed nothing.

hints.text: Compare the job length with typical spot lifetimes.
Step 3 assumes the job runs uninterrupted.
Spot capacity can be reclaimed; work must be resumable.
Consider a reclaim at hour 10.
Step 3 is wrong: interruptions lose progress. Checkpoint.

repair: Checkpoint to object storage every 30 minutes and auto-resume.
debrief: Cheap compute is only cheap if work survives interruptions.

subject: mlops
question: Does running training in another region from the data have no downside?

artifact.description:
Training data (40 TB) is stored in a Mumbai-region bucket. The training cluster runs in a US region, where GPUs are more available, reading the data over the network for each run (weekly).
The data includes Indian customers' personal data.
AI: "Cross-region access is transparent, so this setup has no downside."

ai_claim: Yes. Cloud storage is accessible from any region, so the cluster can read the data transparently with no downside.

ai_solution.text: The bucket can be read from any region.
The cluster reads the data over the network.
Access is transparent.
So there is no downside.

failure.misconception: Ignoring data location, egress and residency
failure.explanation: Reading 40 TB across regions every week incurs large inter-region transfer charges and slow reads, and moving Indian customers' personal data abroad may breach data-residency or contractual requirements. Co-locate compute with data (or use an approved, compliant copy), and check legal requirements before transferring personal data.

canonical_solution: No: weekly 40 TB cross-region reads cost egress, slow training, and may violate data-residency rules. Co-locate compute and data.

valid_evidence.summary: 40 TB x 4 runs per month = 160 TB of inter-region transfer monthly.
Personal data transfers across borders may be restricted by law and contracts.

counterexamples: The monthly transfer bill exceeds the GPU savings.

hints.text: Ask what cross-region reads cost and imply.
Step 3 assumes location does not matter.
Data gravity: move compute to data, especially for personal data.
Compute monthly transfer volume.
Step 3 is wrong: egress costs and residency rules matter.

repair: Train in the data's region (or an approved location) and review residency requirements.
debrief: In ML, data is heavy and regulated. Plan compute around where it lives.

subject: mlops
question: Is the AI right that this configuration balances cost and reliability appropriately?

artifact.description:
Development and staging model endpoints: autoscale 0-2 instances, scaling to zero after 15 minutes without requests (cold start about 40 seconds).
Production endpoint: autoscale 2-10 instances on request rate, never below 2.

ai_claim: Yes. Dev and staging are idle most of the time, so scaling them to zero saves cost, and a 40-second cold start is acceptable there. Production keeps at least 2 instances for availability and no cold starts, and scales with demand.

ai_solution.text: Dev and staging are used intermittently.
Scale-to-zero removes idle cost; cold starts are tolerable for them.
Production keeps a minimum of 2 for redundancy and low latency.
Autoscaling handles production peaks up to 10 instances.

canonical_solution: Correct. Matching scaling policy to each environment's latency and availability needs is good cloud cost practice.

valid_evidence.summary: staging idle 20 h/day -> ~20 instance-hours/day saved; production always has >= 2 instances

hints.text: Compare the needs of dev, staging and production.
Step 3 explains production's minimum.
Scaling policies should reflect each environment's requirements.
Consider a cold start in production.
This solution is correct. The policies fit each environment. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Cost optimisation and reliability are both served by policies tuned per environment.
